title: 7. The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

q.t: What is the probability of an impossible event?
q.e: Impossible sits at the bottom of the 0-to-1 scale.

q.t: What is the probability of a certain event?
q.e: Certain sits at the top of the scale: it happens in every trial.

q.t: A fair coin is tossed. What is P(heads)?
q.e: Two equally likely outcomes, one favourable.

q.t: A fair die is rolled. What is P(4)?
q.e: Six equally likely faces, one of them is 4.

q.t: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called the:
q.e: An event is a subset of this set.

q.t: Which is the sample space for tossing one coin?
q.e: Every possible outcome, each listed once.

q.t: A die rolled 50 times shows 4 eight times. What is the experimental probability of a 4?
q.e: Times it happened ÷ trials = 8/50 = 0.16.

q.t: Which of these is impossible?
o: Rolling a number greater than 6 on a die
q.e: A die has only 1 to 6, so this has probability 0.

q.t: A probability of 0.75 means the event is:
q.e: It's above the 0.5 midpoint but below 1.

q.t: How many outcomes are in the sample space for rolling one die?
A letter is picked at random from PROBABILITY. What is P(B)?
q.e: 11 letters, two of which are B — count every copy.

q.t: Two coins are tossed. What is P(at least one head)?
q.e: {HH, HT, TH} out of {HH, HT, TH, TT}.

q.t: Two coins are tossed. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
q.e: HH, HT, TH, TT — HT and TH are different outcomes.

q.t: A die is rolled. What is P(a number greater than 4)?
A bag has 3 red, 2 blue and 1 green ball. What is P(not red)?
q.e: 3 of the 6 balls are not red.

q.t: In a sample of 30 sweets, 7 are yellow. About how many yellow sweets are in a bag of 600?
q.e: Expected number ≈ probability × population = 7/30 × 600.

q.t: In a sample of 40 students, 9 prefer sports. About how many of the school's 800 students prefer sports?
A coin has landed heads 6 times in a row. P(tails) on the next toss is:
q.e: The coin has no memory — believing tails is 'due' is the gambler's fallacy.

q.t: As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability tends to:
o: Get closer to the theoretical probability
q.e: This is the law of large numbers: streaks get swamped by many results.

q.t: Which experiment has equally likely outcomes?
o: Starting a car: starts or doesn't
A marble from 3 red and 7 blue
q.e: Only the fair die has a symmetry making each outcome equally likely.

q.t: Three coins are tossed. What is P(exactly two heads)?
q.e: {HHT, HTH, THH} out of 8 outcomes.

q.t: A child has 2 shirts and 3 pairs of trousers. How many outfits are possible?
q.e: Each of the 2 shirts goes with each of the 3 trousers: 2 × 3.

q.t: In the word PEACE, what is P(not E)?
q.e: Two of the five cards are E, so three are not.

q.t: A spinner shows 1 to 8, equally likely. What is P(a multiple of 3)?
q.e: Only 3 and 6: 2 out of 8.

q.t: 1000 tyres: 20 lasted under 4000 km, 210 for 4001–9000, 325 for 9001–14000, 445 over 14000. P(between 4000 and 14000 km)?
Basket A has an apple and 2 oranges; basket B a banana and a mango. One fruit from each. P(apple and banana)?
q.e: Six equally likely pairs, one of them is apple–banana (1/3 × 1/2).

q.t: 4 red and 5 blue balls; two drawn without replacement. P(red then blue)?
q.e: Multiply along the branch: 4/9, then 5/8 because one ball has gone.

q.t: Same bag (4 red, 5 blue), without replacement. P(two blue)?
q.e: 5/9, then 4 blue left of 8: 5/9 × 4/8.

q.t: 15 of 50 students like football. The relative frequency is:
q.e: Frequency is 15; relative frequency is 15 ÷ 50.

q.t: Which is a correct sample space for the number of heads when 3 coins are tossed?
q.e: It must include every possible count (0 too) and nothing impossible (like 4).

q.t: Two dice are rolled. What is P(sum is a prime greater than 5)?
q.e: Sum 7 in 6 ways, sum 11 in 2 ways: 8 of 36.

q.t: 4 red, 3 green, 2 blue; two drawn without replacement. P(different colours)?
Three coins: P(first coin heads AND exactly two heads)?
q.e: Only HHT and HTH: 2 of 8.

q.t: A four-digit number uses 1, 2, 3, 4 once each. P(it is even)?
q.e: Only the last digit matters; 2 of the 4 digits are even, each equally likely to be last.

q.t: Guessing 3 questions with 4 options each, P(exactly 2 correct)?
q.e: 3 choices for which one is wrong, each path (1/4)(1/4)(3/4).

q.t: 3 red, 4 black, 2 green pens; you and a friend each pick one WITH replacement. P(same colour)?
Balls 1–4: two draws WITHOUT replacement. How many outcomes in the sample space?
q.e: 4 choices for the first, 3 left for the second; pairs like 1-1 are impossible.

q.t: A dart lands at random on a 3 m × 2 m rectangle containing a circle of diameter 1 m. P(inside the circle)?
q.e: Circle area π × 0.5² = π/4; divide by the rectangle's 6 m².

q.t: Rolling 12 times gave three 3's. Which statement is right?
o: Experimental 1/4 differs from theoretical 1/6 because 12 rolls is few
The next roll is less likely to be 3
q.e: Small samples wobble; with thousands of rolls the relative frequency settles near 1/6.

q.t: With two dice, which event has probability 1?
q.e: Every possible total lies from 1 + 1 = 2 to 6 + 6 = 12.
